name: Tara Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tara, and thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that isn't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a dozer at a big open-pit gold mine. Most of my day is pushing up waste dumps, building the safety berms along the haul roads, and cleaning up the floor of the pit so the trucks don't get flat tyres. It sounds simple, but getting a dump face neat and safe takes a feel you only get after a few years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when I finish a section and it looks right, flat and tidy, and the supervisor doesn't have to say anything. What drains me is the dust in summer and the vibration, my lower back is already telling me off at twenty-seven. My partner Ben works at the same mine, as an electrician in the processing plant, so at least we car-pool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, fair enough. That's not a wild one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise about not much, and move on. I don't really post opinions online, but I'd say it at netball training, probably. People there love a bit of "told you so".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be relieved, but not totally convinced it would stay that way. The mine's already got a couple of remote-controlled dozers for the dangerous dump edges. So the machines are coming either way, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep saving. Ben and I have about three months put away, and we'd like a deposit for a house in two years. I'd maybe use the AI app on my phone a bit more for small stuff, like working out the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady, like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the remote-controlled dozers.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two of them, used on the edges where it's too risky to have someone sitting in the cab. An operator stands at a safe distance with a control box on a strap and drives it. I've had a go, and it's weird, you lose the feel through your seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the budget for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house. We'd like a three-bedroom place in town, near the oval. I've been plugging our numbers into the AI to see how long it takes at different rates, which is about the most I use it for.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of noise about not much and move on. I'd say it at netball training rather than online.
S0.think: I'd be relieved but not convinced it would last, since the mine already uses remote-controlled dozers on dangerous edges. The machines are coming either way, just slower.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving with her partner, who have about three months put away towards a house deposit in two years. Uses an AI app occasionally for small tasks like budgeting.
S0.feel: Calm and steady, much like now.
S0.quote: I've had a go, and it's weird, you lose the feel through your seat.
S0.fieldNote: Her sense of skill is physical, felt through the seat of the dozer, which makes the remote machines feel strange to her. She uses AI in a small, practical way for budgeting. Her main goal is a house in town in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yep, I can see that. Sort of halfway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to learn the new gear, but the company needs to pay for the training and be straight with us about the plan. I'd say that to my supervisor and at the toolbox meeting at the start of shift. I'm not one for big speeches, but I'd ask the questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think dozing is probably in the middle of the list. Trucks first, because they're easy, then drills, then us. So I'd have a few years, and I'd use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the remote dozer training, since it's already on site and proven. I'd also look at what the plant has, because Ben says there are control room jobs over there. We'd keep saving but maybe push the house back a year, to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit unsettled, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel it was proven enough to jump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the remote dozers doing a full shift without needing a person to come rescue them. Right now they get stuck about once a week and someone like me has to go out in a real dozer and pull them free. When that stops, I'll know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with the house if things get worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait. Ben wants to go ahead anyway, he thinks his job's safe. We'd probably argue about it a bit, but I'd want at least six months saved first.

S1.say: I'd say learning the new gear makes sense, but the company should pay for training and be straight about the plan. I'd ask those questions at the toolbox meeting.
S1.think: I think dozing sits in the middle of the list, after trucks and drills. That gives me a few years, and I'd want to use them.
S1.do: Signs up for remote dozer training once it's proven on site and looks into control room jobs in the processing plant. Keeps saving and pushes the house purchase back a year, aiming for six months saved first.
S1.feel: Uneasy and a bit unsettled, but not scared.
S1.quote: Right now they get stuck about once a week and someone like me has to go out in a real dozer and pull them free.
S1.fieldNote: She has a precise test for when to move: the remote dozers running a full shift without rescue. Her steady approach shows in waiting for proof rather than jumping early. There's a small disagreement with her partner about the house that she expects to win with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need someone to slow it down, and that the companies and the government should sit down together and sort out what happens to workers. I'm not really a protest person, but I'd sign things. At the pub I'd be the one saying, let's not panic, let's work out what we can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be out of a job in that picture, maybe within a year of it arriving. Ben might last a bit longer, someone has to wire the robots up. But that's one income, and one income won't get us a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shelve the house completely and get our savings from three months to six as fast as we can. No holiday this year, no new car. I'd start looking at jobs outside mining that need people in person, like the council's road crew or something with the water authority, and I'd ask my uncle, who runs a small earthmoving business, if he needs anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Lots of pressure, but I'd still feel like I could do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough time to save and get my foot in the door somewhere else before everyone else does. If you're first out of the mine, you get the good jobs in town. If you're the hundredth, you get nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, beyond the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger brother, Nico. He's nineteen and just started as a trainee truck driver at the same mine. He's the one I'd lose sleep over, honestly, more than me.

S2.say: I'd say someone needs to slow it down and the companies and government should work out together what happens to workers. I'd sign things and tell people at the pub not to panic.
S2.think: I think I'd be out of a job within about a year of it arriving, while my partner might last a bit longer. One income won't get us a house.
S2.do: Shelves the house plan and pushes savings from three to six months by dropping holidays and a new car. Looks for in-person jobs outside mining, like the council road crew or water authority, and asks her uncle's earthmoving business for work.
S2.feel: Anxious under heavy pressure, but still feeling able to act.
S2.quote: If you're first out of the mine, you get the good jobs in town.
S2.fieldNote: She treats two years as a race to leave before the rush, which is a sharp, practical reading. Her biggest worry is her 19-year-old brother, a trainee truck driver. She avoids protest but would sign petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Hmm. That's more workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a sensible plan, so the companies have no excuse. I'd want the mine to offer training that leads to real jobs, not just certificates. I'd say that in the toolbox meeting too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still a big hit, but five years gives me time to change direction before it lands. The question is which direction. I don't want to pick something that disappears just after I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in the first year, probably the diploma in civil construction supervision, which the mine helps pay for. I'd keep saving and maybe put the house back two years. I'd also talk to my uncle about working with him on weekends, to learn the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a manageable anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why construction supervision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know dirt. I know how ground behaves, how to build a road, how to keep people safe around machines. And somebody's going to have to manage the robots and the people who are left, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to pick something that disappears. How would you check that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at what the people who've already got through it are doing. And I'd probably ask the AI app too, though I'd take what it says with a grain of salt. Then I'd ask Ben, because he's more careful than me.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a sensible plan, so the companies have no excuse. I'd want training that leads to real jobs, not just certificates.
S3.think: I think it's still a big hit, but five years gives me time to change direction before it lands. I'd worry about picking something that disappears just after I finish.
S3.do: Starts a part-time diploma in civil construction supervision in the first year with help from the mine. Keeps saving, delays the house by two years and works weekends with her uncle to learn the business side.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a manageable way.
S3.fieldNote: She builds her plan on what she already knows, ground and machines, and wants training linked to real jobs. She checks decisions with people, an AI app and her partner, in that order. The house keeps getting pushed back as the timeline tightens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no reason anyone should get caught out with ten years' notice. But I'd also say people will still leave it too late, because that's what people do. I'd tell the younger ones to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years makes it manageable for me. I'd have time to get a qualification, save properly and still buy a house. I'd still be a bit worried about Ben and Nico.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the construction supervision diploma over the next three years, then try for a supervisor job at the mine or with the council. We'd go ahead with the house, maybe a year later than planned. I'd keep using the AI app here and there, to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A small worry, mostly in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nico, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to buy that ute on finance he keeps talking about. And I'd tell him to get a trade while he's young, before the driving dries up. He'd ignore me for a year and then do it, that's how he works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold back on, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids, maybe. We'd want them eventually, but I'd want to know I'm in a job that's going to last. Ten years sounds like a lot until you start doing the maths on a mortgage and day care.

S4.say: I'd say nobody should get caught out with ten years' notice, though people will still leave it too late. I'd tell the younger ones to start now.
S4.think: I think ten years makes it manageable for me, with time to qualify, save and still buy a house. I'd still worry about my partner and my brother.
S4.do: Finishes the construction supervision diploma over three years, then applies for supervisor jobs at the mine or council. Buys a house about a year later than planned and keeps using an AI app occasionally to keep up.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with a small worry mostly in the background.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like a lot until you start doing the maths on a mortgage and day care.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she sounds settled, but still delays children until her job feels secure. Her brother remains a thread through every AGI scenario. She plans methodically and expects to follow through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is the mine paying for retraining now, before anything happens, and some kind of income support for a year while you get into new work. And honest notice, so you can make your move early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples who work at the same mine. When it goes, it doesn't just take one of you. It takes the whole household in one go.

headlineQuote: It takes the whole household in one go.
portrait: Tara is a 27-year-old dozer operator at an open-pit gold mine who works at the same site as her partner Ben, an electrician, and they have about three months saved towards a house. She's pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, picks up new tools once they're proven, and has a precise test for when remote dozers are good enough. She's calm in the plateau and uneasy under steady change, then anxious but active in the AGI scenarios, racing to leave early in the two-year case and retraining in construction supervision with five or ten years. Her younger brother, a trainee truck driver, is the person she worries about most.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she expects to lose her job within about a year of it arriving.
whatWouldHelp: The mine paying for retraining now, a year of income support while moving into new work, and honest early notice.
